title: Reveal hidden stored water with state space
equipment: Two interconnected water tanks with inlet pump and two level transmitters
physicalPurpose: Represent both stored-water states and prove why a downstream transfer relation does not contain the current upstream state.
objective: Build an executable state-space model of two interconnected water tanks, predict both internal levels, and demonstrate why one downstream input-output reading cannot reveal all stored water.

simplifications: Equal constant tank areas and linear inter-tank and outlet flow laws
No pump, sensor, overflow, valve, transport-delay, or disturbance dynamics
Both states are measured for teaching, but hidden-state prediction initially reveals only downstream level

baseline.limitation: Identical current downstream readings and inputs do not reveal different upstream stored-water states.

change.decision: Use a state-space representation when internal stored quantities affect future behavior and must remain explicit.

acceptance.window: time of maximum from 0 to 10 s

abortPredicates: Any flow or level is nonfinite
Any tank level leaves 0 through 1 m
The matrix revision, state order, or sample interval differs from the prediction
safety.restorationMode: Set all pump flows to zero and restore all six declared state values
simulationOnlyRestrictions: Physical interconnected tanks require reviewed pump, overflow, low-level, valve, drain, containment, and emergency procedures plus immediate approval.

video.viewerOutcome: Build a physical state-space model and explain why identical output readings can hide different internal futures.

learning.context: An inlet pump feeds two interconnected water tanks with internal upstream and downstream stored-water states.
learning.reason: The input-output view from Lesson 35 does not contain the current internal state and can therefore hide different futures behind the same reading.
theory: A state variable carries the present physical information required to predict future behavior with future input.
State and output equations use declared vectors and matrices whose rows, columns, signs, and units correspond to the two flow balances.
Eigenvalues are natural state modes and relate to transfer-function poles without encoding the current state.
learning.workedPrediction: Calculate 20 cm upstream and 50 cm downstream equilibrium for 0.1 m3/s, then predict a 10.9 cm hidden-state downstream peak near 3.05 s.
practicalPreparation: Verify state order, matrices, units, initial conditions, 100 ms sampling, quality, limits, and Simulation evidence.
Commit the hidden-state future prediction while only identical downstream readings and inputs are visible.
learning.baseline: Observe only pump input and downstream output and explain what internal information is missing.
learning.change: Run the full-state inlet step, restore, compare empty and upstream-charged zero-input cases, then reveal internal states.
learning.comparison: Compare qualified equilibrium errors, downstream separation, charged-case peak and time, and exact matrix-to-balance consistency.
learning.validation: Require 20/50 cm equilibrium, identical hidden downstream initial readings, zero empty response, and approximately 10.9 cm charged peak near 3.05 s.
learning.explanation: State space preserves both stored quantities, whereas a zero-initial-deviation transfer relation cannot reveal water already stored upstream.
learning.transfer: Lesson 37 designs a safe informative experiment before identifying an unknown model.
